title: Ways of reducing the use of resources

notes.definition: Reducing use, reusing and recycling materials reduces the use of limited resources, the use of energy sources, waste and environmental impacts. Glass bottles can be reused or crushed and melted; metals can be melted and recast; scrap steel can be added to iron from the blast furnace.
explanation: Many everyday materials are produced from limited raw materials. Metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics are all made from raw materials that will eventually run out (for example metal ores, sand, limestone, clay and crude oil). In addition, much of the energy used to extract and process these materials comes from limited resources such as fossil fuels. Obtaining raw materials from the Earth by quarrying and mining also causes environmental impacts: it destroys habitats, creates noise, dust and visual scars, and produces large amounts of waste rock.

End users (the people who buy and use products) can help by reducing use, reusing and recycling. Reducing the amount of material used, reusing products and recycling materials reduces the use of limited resources, reduces the use of energy sources, reduces waste (for example less sent to landfill) and reduces environmental impacts.

Some products can be reused. For example, glass bottles can be collected, washed, sterilised and refilled. Glass bottles that are not reused can be crushed and melted to make different glass products, such as new bottles, jars or glass wool insulation. Melting recycled glass needs a lower temperature than making glass from sand, limestone and sodium carbonate, so it saves energy.

Other products cannot be reused and so are recycled for a different use. Metals can be recycled by melting them and recasting or reforming them into different products. The amount of separation required for recycling depends on the material and on the properties required of the final product. For example, some scrap steel can be added to iron from a blast furnace to reduce the amount of iron that needs to be extracted from iron ore. However, metals for high-quality uses must be carefully sorted, because small amounts of other metals can change the properties of the product.

You should be able to evaluate ways of reducing the use of limited resources, given information. Recycling usually uses much less energy than extracting a material from its raw materials (recycling aluminium uses only about 5% of the energy needed to extract it from its ore). But recycling also has costs: materials must be collected, transported and sorted, which uses energy, labour and money. A good evaluation weighs the energy and resources saved against these costs and the impact of mining or landfill.
keyFacts: Reduce, reuse and recycle cuts use of limited resources, energy, waste and environmental impact.
Metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics come from limited raw materials.
Much of the energy for processing comes from limited resources (fossil fuels).
Quarrying and mining cause environmental impacts (habitat loss, noise, dust, waste rock).
Glass bottles can be reused; or crushed and melted to make different glass products.
Metals are recycled by melting and recasting or reforming into different products.
The amount of separation needed depends on the material and the properties required of the final product.
Some scrap steel can be added to iron from the blast furnace, reducing the iron that must be extracted from ore.
Recycling has costs too: collection, transport and sorting.

keyTerms.definition: Use less of a material or product in the first place.
Use a product again for the same or another purpose without reprocessing it, for example refilling a glass bottle.
Reprocess a used material, for example by melting it, so it can be made into a new product.
A raw material that will eventually run out, such as a metal ore or crude oil.
Extracting rock such as limestone or sand from an open pit in the ground.
Used steel that can be melted and added to iron from the blast furnace to make new steel.

workedExamples.title: Energy saved by recycling
workedExamples.question: Producing 1 tonne of aluminium from its ore uses 200 GJ. Recycling uses 5% of this energy. Calculate the energy saved per tonne by recycling.

workedExamples.title: Percentage of glass recycled
workedExamples.question: A town uses 4500 tonnes of glass in a year. 2880 tonnes are collected for recycling. Calculate the percentage recycled.

workedExamples.title: Iron ore saved by using scrap steel
workedExamples.question: A steelworks makes 1000 tonnes of steel. 25% of the iron comes from scrap steel. 1.6 tonnes of iron ore are needed for each tonne of iron extracted. Assuming the steel is almost all iron, calculate the mass of iron ore saved.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think recycling and reusing mean the same thing.
misconceptions.right: In fact reusing keeps the product in its current form (refilling a bottle); recycling reprocesses the material, for example melting glass to make new products.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think recycling has no environmental cost.
misconceptions.right: In fact collecting, transporting and sorting materials uses energy and money, although recycling usually uses less energy than extracting new material.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all scrap metal can be mixed together and melted.
misconceptions.right: In fact the amount of separation needed depends on the material and the properties required; impurities can change the properties of the final product.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think glass and building materials are made from unlimited raw materials.
misconceptions.right: In fact metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics come from limited raw materials.

realWorld: Recycling an aluminium can saves about 95% of the energy needed to make a new can from bauxite ore.
Steelmakers routinely add scrap steel to molten iron from the blast furnace in the basic oxygen process.
Some dairies and breweries still collect, wash and refill glass bottles for reuse.
examTips: When asked how recycling helps, give the four benefits: less use of limited resources, less energy, less waste and fewer environmental impacts (from mining or quarrying).
Use the spec examples: glass bottles reused or crushed and melted; metals melted and recast; scrap steel added to blast furnace iron.
In evaluation questions using data, calculate savings (energy, mass of ore) and also mention the costs of collection and sorting.
Do not confuse reuse with recycling.
summary: Metals, glass, building materials, ceramics and most plastics come from limited raw materials.
Much processing energy comes from limited resources.
Mining and quarrying cause environmental impacts.
Reduce, reuse, recycle cut resource use, energy, waste and impact.
Glass bottles: reused, or crushed and melted for new glass products.
Metals: melted and recast; separation needed depends on use.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of reusing a product?
options: Crushing and melting a glass bottle
Washing and refilling a glass bottle
Melting an aluminium can
Burning a plastic bag for energy
markScheme: 1 mark: washing and refilling a glass bottle
questions.explanation: Reuse keeps the product in its original form. Crushing and melting is recycling.

questions.question: How are metals recycled?
options: Dissolving them in water
Grinding them into powder and burying them
Melting and recasting them into new products
Burning them in air
markScheme: 1 mark: melting and recasting
questions.explanation: Metals can be melted and recast or reformed into different products.

questions.question: Which material is NOT produced from limited raw materials?
options: Steel
Glass
Clay ceramics
Wool from sheep
markScheme: 1 mark: wool from sheep
questions.explanation: Wool is renewable. Metals, glass and clay ceramics come from limited raw materials such as ores, sand and clay.

questions.question: Which is an environmental impact of obtaining raw materials by quarrying?
options: Destruction of habitats and noise
Increased biodiversity
Reduced use of fossil fuels
Less waste rock
markScheme: 1 mark: destruction of habitats and noise
questions.explanation: Quarries remove vegetation and habitats, and blasting and lorries cause noise and dust.

questions.question: Why is some scrap steel added to iron from the blast furnace?
options: To make the iron melt at a higher temperature
To remove carbon from the iron
To make the steel rust faster
To reduce the amount of iron that needs to be extracted from iron ore
markScheme: 1 mark: to reduce the amount of iron extracted from ore
questions.explanation: Recycled scrap steel replaces some newly extracted iron, conserving ore and energy.

questions.question: Why does recycling aluminium save energy compared with extracting it from its ore?
options: Melting aluminium uses much less energy than electrolysis of its ore
Recycled aluminium does not need to be melted
Recycling aluminium releases energy
Aluminium ore is renewable
markScheme: 1 mark: melting uses much less energy than extraction by electrolysis
questions.explanation: Extracting aluminium needs electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide, which uses huge amounts of electricity; melting scrap uses about 5% of that.

questions.question: Why does the amount of sorting needed when recycling metals depend on the final product?
options: All metals melt at the same temperature
Small amounts of other metals can change the properties of the product
Sorting is never needed for metals
Metals cannot be mixed when molten
markScheme: 1 mark: other metals (impurities) change the properties of the product
questions.explanation: For high-specification uses (for example aircraft alloys) the composition must be controlled precisely, so careful separation is needed.

questions.question: A council finds that collecting and sorting a material for recycling uses more energy than making it new. What is the best conclusion?
options: Recycling is always the best option
The material should be made from renewable resources
Collection is unnecessary
Recycling this material may not reduce energy use, so other factors such as resource conservation and landfill must be weighed
markScheme: 1 mark: weigh energy against other factors such as conserving resources and reducing landfill
questions.explanation: Evaluation must balance energy, resource use, waste and cost; recycling is not automatically best for every material.

questions.question: What happens to glass bottles that are collected for recycling (not reuse)?
options: They are crushed and melted to make different glass products
They are washed and refilled
They are buried in landfill
They are dissolved in acid
markScheme: 1 mark: crushed and melted to make different glass products
questions.explanation: Recycling reprocesses the glass. Washing and refilling is reuse.

questions.question: A school throws away 800 kg of waste paper a year. It recycles 520 kg of it. Calculate the percentage of waste paper recycled.
markScheme: 1 mark: 65%

questions.question: Making 1 tonne of new glass from raw materials uses 15 GJ of energy. Using recycled glass reduces this by 30%. Calculate the energy needed to make 1 tonne of glass from recycled glass.
questions.explanation: A 30% reduction leaves 70% of the energy: 0.70 × 15 = 10.5 GJ.

questions.question: Extracting 1 kg of aluminium from its ore uses 210 MJ. Recycling 1 kg uses 5% of this energy. Calculate the energy saved by recycling 50 kg of aluminium.
markScheme: 1 mark: saving per kg = 210 × 0.95 = 199.5 MJ
questions.explanation: Recycling saves 95% of 210 MJ per kg, which is 199.5 MJ, so 50 kg saves 9975 MJ.

questions.question: A copper ore contains 0.8% copper by mass. A recycling centre collects 6 tonnes of scrap copper. Calculate the mass of ore, in tonnes, that would need to be mined to produce the same mass of copper (assume all the copper in the ore is extracted).
markScheme: 1 mark: 750 tonnes
questions.explanation: Recycling 6 tonnes of copper avoids mining 750 tonnes of ore, of which 744 tonnes is waste rock.

questions.question: A glass bottle can be refilled 20 times before it breaks. A town uses 1.2 million bottles of milk a year. Calculate how many new bottles are needed each year if every bottle is reused the maximum number of times. (Each bottle is used once when new, then refilled 20 times.)
markScheme: 1 mark: each bottle gives 21 uses
1 mark: 57 143 bottles (57 000)
questions.explanation: 1 + 20 = 21 uses per bottle. 1 200 000 ÷ 21 = 57 142.9, so about 57 143 new bottles. A common error is dividing by 20.

questions.question: Give two benefits of recycling materials.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: reduces use of limited resources / reduces energy use / reduces waste or landfill / reduces environmental impacts of mining or quarrying
questions.explanation: These are the benefits given in the specification.

questions.question: Name two materials, other than metals, that are produced from limited raw materials.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: glass / building materials / clay ceramics / most plastics
questions.explanation: Glass needs sand, ceramics need clay and most plastics come from crude oil.

questions.question: Explain the difference between reusing and recycling a glass bottle.
markScheme: 1 mark: reusing: the bottle is washed (sterilised) and refilled in the same form
1 mark: recycling: the bottle is crushed and melted to make different glass products
questions.explanation: Reuse uses even less energy than recycling because the glass does not need to be melted.

questions.question: Explain why using less of a product reduces the use of energy from limited resources.
markScheme: 1 mark: fewer products or less material need to be extracted and manufactured
1 mark: extraction and manufacture use energy, much of which comes from fossil fuels (limited resources)
questions.explanation: Every stage of making a product uses energy, so making less saves energy.

questions.question: Give two disadvantages of recycling.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: collection and transport use energy / sorting and separating is difficult or costly / needs labour / recycled material may be lower quality
questions.explanation: Recycling has costs that must be weighed against its benefits.

questions.question: Scrap steel from cars is often mixed with other metals such as copper from wiring. Explain why the amount of separation required depends on the steel product being made.
markScheme: 1 mark: other metals (impurities) change the properties of the steel
1 mark: products that need specific properties (for example high-strength steel) require careful separation
1 mark: products with less demanding requirements (for example reinforcing bars) can use less carefully separated scrap
questions.explanation: The specification states that the amount of separation depends on the material and the properties required of the final product.

questions.question: State one environmental impact of mining for metal ores.
markScheme: 1 mark: any one of: destroys habitats / noise / dust / large amounts of waste rock / scars the landscape / water pollution
questions.explanation: Mining disturbs large areas of land and produces waste.

questions.question: Suggest why reusing a glass bottle saves more energy than recycling it.
markScheme: 1 mark: reuse only needs washing/sterilising
1 mark: recycling requires crushing and melting at high temperature, which uses much more energy
questions.explanation: The less the product is reprocessed, the less energy is needed.

questions.question: Describe how glass bottles and metal cans can be reused or recycled, and explain how this reduces the use of resources.
markScheme: Indicative content: glass bottles can be collected, washed and refilled (reuse); glass not reused is crushed and melted to make different glass products; metal cans are melted and recast or reformed into different products; this reduces quarrying of sand and limestone and mining of ores; less energy (from fossil fuels) needed; less waste in landfill; fewer environmental impacts.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes reuse or recycling for both materials and clearly explains at least two ways this reduces resource use.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple description of recycling or one benefit.
questions.explanation: Link each method to the specific resources and energy saved.

questions.question:
A local council is deciding whether to start collecting aluminium cans, glass bottles and plastic food trays for recycling.
Information:
Aluminium: recycling saves 95% of extraction energy; cans are easy to separate with magnets and eddy currents.
Glass: recycling saves about 30% of energy; must be sorted by colour.
Plastic trays: several different polymers that are hard to separate; recycled plastic is often lower quality.
Evaluate the benefits and drawbacks of collecting each material, and recommend which the council should prioritise.
markScheme: Indicative content: aluminium: very large energy saving because extraction uses electrolysis; easy separation; conserves bauxite; high priority. Glass: moderate energy saving; reduces quarrying of sand and limestone; sorting by colour adds cost; bottles could be reused instead; glass is heavy so transport uses fuel. Plastic: conserves crude oil and reduces landfill; but separation of polymers is difficult and costly; lower quality product. General: collection and transport use energy, labour and money; reduces waste and environmental impact of mining and quarrying. Recommendation, for example aluminium first, then glass, plastic last unless separation improves.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed evaluation of all three materials using the information, considering both benefits and costs, with a justified recommendation.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some evaluation of at least two materials, with a recommendation partly justified.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about recycling, for example 'saves energy'.
questions.explanation: Use the information given, compare the size of the savings, and weigh them against the difficulty of separation and collection.

questions.question: Which action is an example of 'reduce'?
options: Melting old cans to make new cans
Using thinner aluminium to make each can
Refilling a milk bottle
Sending glass to a bottle bank
markScheme: 1 mark: using thinner aluminium to make each can
questions.explanation: Reducing means using less material in the first place. Melting cans is recycling; refilling is reuse.

questions.question: State where much of the energy used to extract and process materials comes from.
markScheme: 1 mark: fossil fuels / limited (finite) resources
questions.explanation: Most industrial energy comes from burning coal, oil and natural gas, which are limited.

questions.question: Which statement explains why some products are recycled rather than reused?
options: Recycling always uses less energy than reuse
Reused products are always unsafe
Some products cannot be reused in their current form, so the material is recycled for a different use
Recycling does not require any collection
markScheme: 1 mark: some products cannot be reused so are recycled for a different use
questions.explanation: For example, a drinks can cannot be refilled and resealed, so its metal is melted and made into new products.
